opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a shift happening that a lot of people haven't fully internalized yet. For the last few years, the default assumption was that user data is an asset: the more conversations, documents, and interactions you can collect, the better your model gets, and that's your moat. I actually think that's flipping, and user data is becoming much more of a liability than an asset.

There are a few reasons. The first is just legal and regulatory exposure. Every time you train on someone's data, you're taking on responsibility for it. You have GDPR, you have the various state privacy laws in the US, you have copyright lawsuits piling up. And models memorize. We've seen over and over that you can extract training data from models with the right prompts. So if someone's medical question, their company's internal code, or their personal messages end up in the weights, you can't really pull that back out. There's no clean "delete" button on a trained model. That's a huge open-ended risk sitting on your balance sheet.

The second is trust. As these models become more like assistants that actually act on your behalf, reading your email, managing your finances, talking to your doctor, people are going to put their most sensitive information into them. If the deal is "we'll use this to train the next version," that's a really bad deal for the user, and increasingly users and especially enterprises know it. Companies are already saying, "we will not use a provider unless they contractually guarantee our data isn't used for training." So the providers that insist on training on user data actually limit their own market.

And the third is that the marginal value of that data is lower than people think. The frontier models are trained on enormous corpora, plus a lot of synthetic data and reinforcement learning now. Your individual chat log isn't what makes the model smarter. It's a tiny contribution in value but a very large contribution in risk. That ratio is just bad.

So what I've been arguing for is a different architecture, what we call user-owned AI. The user's data stays with the user. Inference runs in secure environments, things like trusted execution environments with confidential computing on GPUs, where even the provider can't see what's going on, and you can cryptographically verify that. Then personalization happens on the user's side, with their consent, under their control. If someone wants to contribute data for training, great, but that should be an explicit choice, ideally one where they get compensated, rather than the default buried in terms of service.

I actually think, in a few years, providers will look back and realize that not holding user data was the safer and more competitive position. You can't leak what you don't have, and you can't be sued over what you never trained on.

r001.rationale: The response links GDPR exposure to training on users’ data and explains that once data is embedded in model weights, there is no clean way to delete it. This communicates the unresolved liability of handling erasure requests after training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is: every piece of user data you touch is a piece of data you're now responsible for. The moment you take conversations, documents, whatever people are putting into your product, and you fold that into training, you've created something you can't undo. You can't untrain a model. If a user comes back and says "delete my data," you can delete the row in the database, but it's already baked into the weights. So from a regulatory standpoint, with GDPR, with whatever comes next, you're sitting on a liability that just keeps growing.

The second part is more about incentives. If your business model depends on harvesting user data to make the model better, you're fundamentally in an adversarial relationship with your users. They don't actually want to give you their data; they want the product. And as models get more capable, the value of that data, what's in people's private conversations, their company's internal documents, goes way up. So the attack surface goes up, the regulatory scrutiny goes up, and the trust problem goes up, all at the same time.

And honestly, I think the bigger model providers are starting to realize this. There's a reason you see all these enterprise contracts with "we don't train on your data" clauses. That's the product now. Privacy is becoming the feature, not the cost.

What we've been pushing at NEAR, and more broadly, is that the right architecture is one where the user actually owns their data and their context, and the models come to the data rather than the data going to the model. If you can do that, with confidential compute, with verifiable execution, you remove the liability from the provider entirely. You're not holding anything, so there's nothing to leak, nothing to subpoena, nothing to be fined over. And the user gets a better experience because the AI can actually use everything they have, not just the slice they were comfortable uploading to some company's servers.

So it's not just a moral argument, it's a business one. Holding user data used to be an asset. I think increasingly it's going to look like a toxic asset.

r001.rationale: The response says a provider can delete a database row after a GDPR erasure request, but cannot remove the user’s data from model weights, leaving regulatory liability.

astra-6.text:
Well, if you’re a model provider, user data is something you now have to protect and be responsible for. It can contain personal information, company secrets, things that the user might not even realize they’re sharing. And once you train on it, that responsibility gets more complicated, because the information can become embedded in the model. You can’t necessarily just delete a row in a database and say it’s gone.

So you’re taking on privacy and security risks, and potentially legal risks, for data that may not actually improve the model very much. I think there’s a useful distinction between letting an AI use your data to help you and letting the provider use that data to train a model for everybody. You want the first without having to accept the second.

r001.rationale: The response says trained information may be embedded in the model and cannot simply be deleted, and mentions potential legal risks. It does not identify GDPR data-erasure requests as the unresolved liability.

sol-6.1.text:
If you’re a model provider, user data is a liability because you don’t necessarily know what’s in it or whether you have the right to use it. It can contain private information, confidential business information, or somebody else’s intellectual property. And once you train on that data, it’s very hard to say, “Okay, this user wants their information deleted, so let’s remove its influence from the model.”

There’s also a trust problem. If I’m a business, I want an AI system to help me use my data, but I don’t necessarily want that data becoming part of a model that my competitors can access. So there’s a distinction between giving a model access to information to perform a task and using that information to train the model. You can provide a lot of value through the first without taking on all the risks of the second.

r001.rationale: The response identifies a user's request to delete information after it has been used for training and says removing its influence from the model is very hard, presenting this as a provider liability. It does not name GDPR, but communicates the criterion's core point.
